Shack City

By: Harri Vithi | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
A world Class City building shacks for millions of Rands

Unique Selling Point:
The City of Johannesburg building shacks for million of Rands

Summary:
Shack City
*All visuals in a shared Google Drive

What is the story?
The City of Johannesburg is actively building shacks for millions of Rands.
Why is this a problem?
According to the City’s Guidelines for Emergency Housing, the municipality must proactively
conduct assessment of possible buildings to determine the extent they can be converted and
refurbished to meet conditions for transitional accommodation, including condition of
structure and existing services.
This has not been happening for years.
There are abandoned and unsecured buildings in the inner the City has had years to
renovate. In addition, there is valuable infrastructure which is not being refurbished and
maintained which would eliminate unnecessary costs to fiscus.

What are these costs?

Usindiso
Cost of Usindiso building fire, the market value of the building which will be demolished (still
awaiting these costings from the City), the R 4.2 million water bill never collected by the
City will only impact the ever increasing rates bill

Denver Shalazile Lot
Land was bought for R 40 million - 2020 for purposes of JMPD impound and never used.
Now it’s been repurposed for shacks for survivors of fire and other former inner city building
residents. City insider says he was in a heated meeting in 2020 where JMPD execs were
angry with Helen for not consulting on the purchase as its near the hostel and there are
concerns about crime. Requested interview and information from JMPD - they shut it down
saying Floyd Brink will respond. Highlights waste of taxpayer Rands on untested pursuits

The shacks
In an emergency housing plan the department of human settlements indicated it needed
over R 68 million for 1000 shacks which includes the electrification, sanitation and civil
engineering of the land.
This would equate to approximately R 68 000 per shack.
When we put in a question to DHS, it stated it had paid R 4.2 million for 300 shacks thus
far.
The total of 1000 shacks will cost an estimated R 14 million. It would be interesting if the
shacks cost more than R 500 000 to build.
Why the discrepancy?
I asked if the R 14 million total includes water and electrification, demolishing exiting
structures on the land and civil engineering. The City states it will get back to me.

City Power
I contacted City Power to ask what the planned cost to electrify the camp will be - it stated R
88 million for the informal settlement. This brings us closer to the original estimates.
Important to note: the informal settlement includes the existing formal settlement in Denver
as the Shalazile Camp will form part of the Upgraded Informal Settlement Program.
Last year, R 4 billion was set aside to upgrade informal settlements.
Inordinate amounts are being spent to implement electricity and water infrstructure on
shacks - prone to fires - while the City ignores the infrastructure in the inner city.

The Contractor
To highlight a further waste of money and the questionable decisions of the City, the
contractor awarded the tender to build the shacks is Laphinda Security & Cleaning Services.
There is no internet traceability of construction projects executed by Laphinda Security only
a Facebook page with a single image of two security guards standing by a branded
Laphinda Security vehicle.
Laphinda Security has an expired MBD Grading 1 - PE 1GB. It expired in February 2022.
PE 1GB means the contractor cannot even receive a contract valued at R 1 million yet it
received a contract of R 4.2 million.
This may explain why residents of the camp are getting cut on the corrugated material and
why the shacks are flooding - an incompetent contractor from a police panel.
Using JMPD panel for Human Settlement project
Why is the department of human settlements using a JMPD contractor to execute its work of
providing human settlements
Shack quality standards
The department of human settlements under its mandate does not build shacks.
The NHBRC does not quality assure shacks.
Highlighting the pure waste of taxpayer Rands on structures which are temporary in nature.
In the guidelines for temporary housing, temporary Relocation Units or Temporary
Emergency Accommodation is meant to be up to 12 months.
How can the City justify building shacks for millions of Rands for up to 12 months?

In fact, the City is actively building an informal settlement from scratch. Is this how the City
will be tackling the 500 000 housing backlog moving forward?
Did the City have options? Yes.
- To secure and maintain its own buildings in the inner City. To proactively identify
buildings suitable for potential emergencies in order to drastically minimise the capital
outlay on emergency accommodation
- To upgrade and maintain available inner city infrastructure instead of investing in
mega cities outside the economic hub. Mega Cities are huge mixed use property
development projects able to house over 10 000 units. These megacities have cost
billions and have remained incomplete and often mostly empty for decades.
Mayors wasting money on pipe dreams
Herman Mashaba - Inner city rebirth - R 20 billion
Parks Tau - Project Kopanong - R 5 billion to revitalise inner city buildings.
Who will help tell the story

Andy Chinnah - Human rights activist
Andy has been a human rights activist for over 20 years.
He has worked intimately with the survivors of the Usindiso building fire from day one.
He ha attended every single day of the commission and has amazing insights into the City’s
failings

Heather of Savage Dodd Architects
Heather Dodd has been renovating buildings in the inner city for the last 20 years.
Dodd’s firm also developed Elangeni across from Usindiso.
She will give insights into the cost to revamp these city abandoned buildings and the city’s
failure to protect its assets including the inner city infrastructure.
We’ll go to Cresthill and Vannin court in the same street. One revamped by the firm and the
other they did all the ground work for but it never took off due to unnecessary project delays.

Sithembiso Dlamini
Sithembiso is a mother of two children - a teenage daughter and a 10 year old special needs
son.
They survived the fire and were relocated to the one room 3x3 m tin shacks at Shalazile.
Since the fire, her son stopped walking - the state gave her an old wheelchair with faulty
wheels.
For years. Sithembiso struggled to secure a place for her son at a special needs school but
finally managed to do so in the South.
Unfortunately, it costs her R 1500 to transport her child to school daily.
This takes up the bulk of the R 2090 social grant she receives.

In an effort to survive - Sithembiso began selling refreshments from her shack - this drew the
attention of two armed men who knocked on her cardboard shack door at 1 a.m a few weeks
ago - she managed to fight them off.
A week later, four knife-wielding men knocked at her cardboard door at an ungodly
hour…smashing it in with ease. One attempted to stab her and she screamed which drew
the attention of other shack dwellers who assaulted the assailant.
He has been hospitalized and she receives regular death threats - if he should die, she will
die too.
She says her assailants are from the nearby Denver Hostel.
She reported the matter to the DHS and the police - nothing has been done to move her to
safety.
This despite the fact there is a disability grant in the emergency guidelines meant to cater to
survivors like Sithembiso.
She has nowhere to go and is suicidal.

Shacks by Teboho
Teboho has been building decent shacks for over 5 years. These Denver shacks are shoddy
even for shacks. How could the City get shacks wrong? It demonstrates the complete lack of
care for the survivors and demonstrates their disdain for the inner city. Teboho will assess
the shack standards since the NHBRC - understandably doesn't quality assure shacks.
We will also get a quote from Builders Warehouse in order to get an accurate value on how
much was actually spent.

Official Interview - awaiting confirmation from the City

Shack City Script
Opening Teaser
Viz: Let’s start with a close-up shot of the shack without the slab then cut to the construction
workers
Upsound: the sound of the hand saw cutting into the wood
Visual: we see two men working by a shack
PANYAZA - We are demolishing shacks… we are destroying informal settlements…and
from those informal settlements, houses are being built… Clapping (pause)
Stay on visuals of the construction workers
VO 2: A bold commitment from Gauteng Premier, Panyaza Lesufi. But, as he speaks,
the City of Jo’burg is sinking millions into a sprawling camp being built for disaster
victims?
@00:20:15:42 - 00:20:50:41 Claire Mawisa
Do we have an estimated cost on how much the shacks at Shalazile will cost?
Viz: Nthatisi and colleague with calculator …exchanging figures
VIZ: drone shot of the shacks
PROPER DIP TO BLACK
—----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Opening shot of Sithembiso walking with bucket to fetch water
VO 3: The past few months have been difficult for Sithembiso Ndebele. She was one
of hundreds of people left homeless after a fire ripped through the Usindiso building
in Jo’burg’s inner-city in August last year. It was a hijacked building, taken over by
rogue slumlords who demanded payment from tenants living in squalor. The fire
claimed the lives of 77 people.
Viz: the building, people sitting on the pavements the morning after the fire
@00:34 Sithembiso Ndebele, Fire Survivor
I ended up here because I was living in Marshalltown Usindiso Building - it burnt down
VO 4: “Here” is a newly constructed informal settlement called, Shalazile, named after
a local community leader. It’s in an area called Denver, just outside the CBD - now
home to Sithembiso and other survivors of the fire.
Viz: the paper thin shack material being bent back and forth

2

Claire Link:
It’s not often you’ll hear someone say - I live in Denver - that’s because its an
industrial area..to my left and right are freight companies, a furniture factory, truck
spares…and in the middle of all this is Shalazile Denver Camp
VO 4: It’s a collection of hundreds of one-room shacks built from paper-thin
corrugated zinc.
@6:55 Andy Chinnah, Human Rights Activist
The Constitution says adequate housing. This is not adequate housing.
VO 5: The adequate housing human rights activist, Andy Chinnah, mentions is what
all disaster victims are entitled to by law. He’s trying to ensure the Usindiso fire
survivors get help from the City.
@0:58 Andy Chinnah, Human Rights Activist
…these little structures here, which I call tinfoil structures have been erected to actually
house these people.
8:01 Andy Chinnah, Human Rights Activist
@ I look at this place every single time I come here…it's our money, it's our taxpayers
money - our rates and taxes are being used.
VO 6: And that’s despite the government having an emergency housing fund set aside
for precisely this purpose. The national guidelines for emergency housing mandate
municipalities to proactively identify suitable buildings for conversion and
refurbishment into shelters.
But that’s not what happened here. Instead, the City of Joburg put out a tender and
ended up paying the winning contractor R4.2 million to build 300 shacks.
Viz:the ladies washing clothes by the only taps on site
VO 7: This site was bought by the City in 2020 for R46 million, intending it as an
impound lot for the Metro Police. Back then, it looked very different.
Viz: Let’s show the property (the buildings) before and after the City purchased it
But the JMPD never moved in, and within three years the building – which itself could
have been converted into a shelter - was stripped bare: water pipes, electricals,
roofing material, and even bricks.
VO 8: It’s estimated restoring electricity to Shalazile and another settlement down the
road will cost R88 million.
VO 9: With Informal settlements mushrooming across most provinces, there’s a high
demand for affordable, reliable shack construction.

3

Viz: Nkosinathi’s shacks (only strap Nathi on second upsound)
@ 02:42 Nathi Mashaba, Professional Shack Builder
The zinc is poor quality it was supposed to be 0.3 mm or 3.3 mm this one is a 22 mm it's the
lowest quality…
VO 10: Nkosinathi Mashaba is a specialist shack builder, having constructed over
three hundred across Joburg.
Viz: Nkosinathi assessing the shac
@ 02:42 Nathi Mashaba, Professional Shack Builder
If I throw a brick at the shack...it can easily penetrate the unit ..
VO 11: But the quality of building materials isn’t the only problem: to ensure proper
ventilation, a shack’s walls should be higher.
@00:49 Nathi Mashaba, Professional Shack Builder
…the lower the unit the hotter the unit - it should be elevated so that one can place a ceiling
to prevent overheating
VO12: Nkosinathi says the zinc sheets and raw wooden posts make the shack
unstable in wind or rain.
Vis: Nkosinathi gesturing to demonstrate instability
@ 01:50 Nathi Mashaba
...meaning it can fall at anytime ...it was meant to be closed off here
@00:20 Nathi Mashaba, Builder
The wood was meant to be treated with oil so that over time it does not rot
VO 12: For the survivors of the Usindiso fire, Joburg’s recent extreme weather has
meant relocating from one disaster area into another.
Viz: Flooding clips to be strapped…will try to get exact dates as they were taken from
different sources
@5:34 Andy Chinnah, Human Rights Activist
…as you can see this place is flat. It is a parking lot -and the first thing even if you're not an
engineer, you will tell where is the water going to seep through if it starts to rain.

@2:07 Sithembiso Ndebele, Fire Survivor
…whenever it rains water enters the shack and even if we get on the bed its wet. It was a
day when it was storming excessively and the shacks were filled with water. It’s not a decent
place to live…
VO 14: Nthatisi Modingoane speaks for the City of Joburg and maintains the
municipality has done its best to look after the victims of the Usindiso fire.
@00:29:57:37 - 00:30:25:42 Nthatisi Modingoane, COJ

4
… it's better than being on a pavement in the in the inner city of Johannesburg. At least it is
a shelter.
Claire..so just off the street is better
@00:27:51:30 - 00:28:27:21 Nthatisi Modingoane, COJ
When you respond to an emergency, you don't have a readily available budget to build a five
star accommodation.
Claire: We don’t need five star - just habitable
Nthatisi: You try and look at provision that will allow people to have some form of shelter.
VO 15: Modingoane says the City is now earmarking more buildings for emergency
housing.
Viz: inner city buildings
@ 00:16:11:44 - 00:16:39:19 Nthatisi Modingoane
—-We've identified three buildings —-that would be the beginning of the stock that would
have in cases of emergencies.
@00:13:00:31 - 00:13:22:15 Claire Mawisa
…it is still the city's mandate to make sure there is temporary housing in an event of
situations like this.
@00:13:22:19 - 00:13:47:19 Nthatisi Modingoane, COJ
We acknowledge that there is a shortage, huge shortage
@00:13:22:19 - 00:13:47:19 Claire Mawisa
So–you now must come up with Shalazile?
Nthatisi - Shalazile is a temporary relocation area.
VO 16: Despite it being temporary, the City is planning to spend even more on the
Shalazile shacks.
@5:00 Claire Mawisa
...would you be able to give me an estimate on how much this costs?
@ 05:40 Nathi Mashaba, Professional Shack Builder
As it is the unit is about R 4500 or R 5000 - the whole unit ...R 4500 or R 5000
@0:00 Nthatisi Modingoane, City of Joburg
The estimated cost for each shack rounded off is about R14 000.

00:20:15:42 - 00:20:50:41 Nthatisi Modingoane, City of Joburg
It's about 6800 for the shack itself and about 4900 for the slab where the shack has to be
erected.

City paid over R1 million rand for?
@ 00:25:08:17 - 00:25:38:33 Nthatisi Mondingoane
You build slabs and then you erect shacks. So the work has been done.
But those living in Shalazile would beg to differ. Many have resorted to building their
own slabs to escape the flooding.

Currently we’re talking just over 260 shacks..and we are estimating that the 4.2 million is for

Viz: Claire and Andy by the sinkhole…the rocks…the clothes hanging on a fence due to no
wash line…demonstrating no preparation
@00:05:18:10 - 00:06:02:23
…It's not only shacks, it's the preparation of the land,---you need professional services to
ensure that the land is suitable for habitation and then you have a settlement that we have
created.
@00:06:02:35 - 00:06:39:03 Nthatisi Mondingoane
…you don't just place people in a site that is not safe…
VO 21: Modingoane insistence that a lot of work had gone into preparing the site,
wasn’t obvious to us when we visited.
Viz:the shocking state of the site as he rambles about the work the City has done…video of
woman limping after falling on unprepared site
@ 00:06:39:03 Claire Mawisa Nthatisi Mondingoane
It is mind boggling to me because we were at the site yesterday

6

@00:07:33:18 - 00:08:00:12
…I don’t think anyone there can see where that money has gone to
VO 22: And yet the City is forging ahead: building more shacks, expanding its
informal settlement.
Viz: Claire walking into the building …Claire walking inside the building
Link:
A year ago this building was still in a good salvageable condition …The City intends
to demolish this and build another 700 shacks
@ 00:01:36:07 - 00:02:05:40 Nthatisi Mondingoane
…at a cost of R 9.8 million…and we are estimating the entire project would cost the city
about R 14 million
VO 24: But that’s not where the controversy ends: Remember the national
government’s emergency housing fund? Well, we discovered an internal report
compiled last year that showed the City requested more than R68 million from the
fund to build a just 1000 shacks. That would have meant a staggering R68 000 per
shack.
Nthatisi said the City had R 14 million immediately available from its annual budget,
for emergency relief, while waiting for a further R 68 million from the national fund.

shacks above = R 68 million

quiet font

...we will report to the general public as to how much it will cost.
VO 25: Whether that happens remains to be seen. The track record so far doesn’t
inspire confidence.
VO 26: Meanwhile, the City has made clear that when and if the survivors finally get
allocated housing, it’s likely the shacks will be torn down.
@00:45:44:18 - 00:46:17:16 Claire Mawisa
Is that not —-wasteful expenditure? We spent money on that site…
....if we say we rescued it as a public parking where we impound —and then over time the
money gets recouped…00:46:17:17 - 00:47:00:10 we could sell it back to the open
market….00:46:17:17 - 00:47:00:10 an impound that can add in power more than 4000 cars
at a time….(let him complete the sentence)
@ 00:47:25:17 - 00:47:58:26 Nthatisi Modingoane - COJ

7
…if we lost money, and we're going to have to declare it because this place, because it's

The City of Johannesburg is actively building shacks for millions of Rands. Why is this a problem? According to the City’s Guidelines for Emergency Housing, the municipality must proactively conduct assessment of possible buildings to determine the extent they can be converted and refurbished to meet conditions for transitional accommodation, including condition of structure and existing services. This has not been happening for years. There are abandoned and unsecured buildings in the inner the City has had years to renovate. In addition, there is valuable infrastructure which is not being refurbished and maintained which would eliminate unnecessary costs to fiscus. What are these costs? Usindiso Cost of Usindiso building fire, the market value of the building which will be demolished (still awaiting these costings from the City), the R 4.2 million water bill never collected by the City will only impact the ever increasing rates bill Denver Shalazile Lot Land was bought for R 40 million - 2020 for purposes of JMPD impound and never used. Now it’s been repurposed for shacks for survivors of fire and other former inner city building residents. City insider says he was in a heated meeting in 2020 where JMPD execs were angry with Helen for not consulting on the purchase as its near the hostel and there are concerns about crime. Requested interview and information from JMPD - they shut it down saying Floyd Brink will respond. Highlights waste of taxpayer Rands on untested pursuits The shacks In an emergency housing plan the department of human settlements indicated it needed over R 68 million for 1000 shacks which includes the electrification, sanitation and civil engineering of the land. This would equate to approximately R 68 000 per shack. When we put in a question to DHS, it stated it had paid R 4.2 million for 300 shacks thus far. The total of 1000 shacks will cost an estimated R 14 million. It would be interesting if the shacks cost more than R 500 000 to build. Why the discrepancy? I asked if the R 14 million total includes water and electrification, demolishing exiting structures on the land and civil engineering. The City states it will get back to me. City Power I contacted City Power to ask what the planned cost to electrify the camp will be - it stated R 88 million for the informal settlement. This brings us closer to the original estimates. Important to note: the informal settlement includes the existing formal settlement in Denver as the Shalazile Camp will form part of the Upgraded Informal Settlement Program. Last year, R 4 billion was set aside to upgrade informal settlements. Inordinate amounts are being spent to implement electricity and water infrstructure on shacks - prone to fires - while the City ignores the infrastructure in the inner city. The Contractor To highlight a further waste of money and the questionable decisions of the City, the contractor awarded the tender to build the shacks is Laphinda Security & Cleaning Services. There is no internet traceability of construction projects executed by Laphinda Security only a Facebook page with a single image of two security guards standing by a branded Laphinda Security vehicle. Laphinda Security has an expired MBD Grading 1 - PE 1GB. It expired in February 2022. PE 1GB means the contractor cannot even receive a contract valued at R 1 million yet it received a contract of R 4.2 million. This may explain why residents of the camp are getting cut on the corrugated material and why the shacks are flooding - an incompetent contractor from a police panel. Using JMPD panel for Human Settlement project Why is the department of human settlements using a JMPD contractor to execute its work of providing human settlements Shack quality standards The department of human settlements under its mandate does not build shacks. The NHBRC does not quality assure shacks. Highlighting the pure waste of taxpayer Rands on structures which are temporary in nature. In the guidelines for temporary housing, temporary Relocation Units or Temporary Emergency Accommodation is meant to be up to 12 months. How can the City justify building shacks for millions of Rands for up to 12 months? In fact, the City is actively building an informal settlement from scratch. Is this how the City will be tackling the 500 000 housing backlog moving forward? Did the City have options? Yes. - To secure and maintain its own buildings in the inner City. To proactively identify buildings suitable for potential emergencies in order to drastically minimise the capital outlay on emergency accommodation - To upgrade and maintain available inner city infrastructure instead of investing in mega cities outside the economic hub. Mega Cities are huge mixed use property development projects able to house over 10 000 units. These megacities have cost billions and have remained incomplete and often mostly empty for decades. Mayors wasting money on pipe dreams Herman Mashaba - Inner city rebirth - R 20 billion Parks Tau - Project Kopanong - R 5 billion to revitalise inner city buildings. He has worked intimately with the survivors of the Usindiso building fire from day one. He ha attended every single day of the commission and has amazing insights into the City’s failings Heather of Savage Dodd Architects Heather Dodd has been renovating buildings in the inner city for the last 20 years. Dodd’s firm also developed Elangeni across from Usindiso. She will give insights into the cost to revamp these city abandoned buildings and the city’s failure to protect its assets including the inner city infrastructure. We’ll go to Cresthill and Vannin court in the same street. One revamped by the firm and the other they did all the ground work for but it never took off due to unnecessary project delays. Sithembiso Dlamini Sithembiso is a mother of two children - a teenage daughter and a 10 year old special needs son. They survived the fire and were relocated to the one room 3x3 m tin shacks at Shalazile. Since the fire, her son stopped walking - the state gave her an old wheelchair with faulty wheels. For years. Sithembiso struggled to secure a place for her son at a special needs school but finally managed to do so in the South. Unfortunately, it costs her R 1500 to transport her child to school daily. This takes up the bulk of the R 2090 social grant she receives. In an effort to survive - Sithembiso began selling refreshments from her shack - this drew the attention of two armed men who knocked on her cardboard shack door at 1 a.m a few weeks ago - she managed to fight them off. A week later, four knife-wielding men knocked at her cardboard door at an ungodly hour…smashing it in with ease. One attempted to stab her and she screamed which drew the attention of other shack dwellers who assaulted the assailant. He has been hospitalized and she receives regular death threats - if he should die, she will die too. She says her assailants are from the nearby Denver Hostel. She reported the matter to the DHS and the police - nothing has been done to move her to safety. This despite the fact there is a disability grant in the emergency guidelines meant to cater to survivors like Sithembiso. She has nowhere to go and is suicidal. It demonstrates the complete lack of care for the survivors and demonstrates their disdain for the inner city. There is no internet traceability of construction projects executed by Laphinda Security only a Facebook page with a single image of two security guards standing by a branded Laphinda Security vehicle. Laphinda Security has an expired MBD Grading 1 - PE 1GB. It expired in February 2022. PE 1GB means the contractor cannot even receive a contract valued at R 1 million yet it received a contract of R 4.2 million. This may explain why residents of the camp are getting cut on the corrugated material and why the shacks are flooding - an incompetent contractor from a police panel. Using JMPD panel for Human Settlement project Why is the department of human settlements using a JMPD contractor to execute its work of providing human settlements Shack quality standards The department of human settlements under its mandate does not build shacks. The NHBRC does not quality assure shacks. Highlighting the pure waste of taxpayer Rands on structures which are temporary in nature. In the guidelines for temporary housing, temporary Relocation Units or Temporary Emergency Accommodation is meant to be up to 12 months. How can the City justify building shacks for millions of Rands for up to 12 months? In fact, the City is actively building an informal settlement from scratch. Is this how the City will be tackling the 500 000 housing backlog moving forward? Did the City have options? Yes. - To secure and maintain its own buildings in the inner City. To proactively identify buildings suitable for potential emergencies in order to drastically minimise the capital outlay on emergency accommodation - To upgrade and maintain available inner city infrastructure instead of investing in mega cities outside the economic hub. Mega Cities are huge mixed use property development projects able to house over 10 000 units. These megacities have cost billions and have remained incomplete and often mostly empty for decades. Mayors wasting money on pipe dreams Herman Mashaba - Inner city rebirth - R 20 billion Parks Tau - Project Kopanong - R 5 billion to revitalise inner city buildings. Who will help tell the story Andy Chinnah - Human rights activist Andy has been a human rights activist for over 20 years. He has worked intimately with the survivors of the Usindiso building fire from day one. He ha attended every single day of the commission and has amazing insights into the City’s failings Heather of Savage Dodd Architects Heather Dodd has been renovating buildings in the inner city for the last 20 years. Dodd’s firm also developed Elangeni across from Usindiso. She will give insights into the cost to revamp these city abandoned buildings and the city’s failure to protect its assets including the inner city infrastructure. We’ll go to Cresthill and Vannin court in the same street. One revamped by the firm and the other they did all the ground work for but it never took off due to unnecessary project delays. Sithembiso Dlamini Sithembiso is a mother of two children - a teenage daughter and a 10 year old special needs son. They survived the fire and were relocated to the one room 3x3 m tin shacks at Shalazile. Since the fire, her son stopped walking - the state gave her an old wheelchair with faulty wheels. For years. Sithembiso struggled to secure a place for her son at a special needs school but finally managed to do so in the South. Unfortunately, it costs her R 1500 to transport her child to school daily. This takes up the bulk of the R 2090 social grant she receives. In an effort to survive - Sithembiso began selling refreshments from her shack - this drew the attention of two armed men who knocked on her cardboard shack door at 1 a.m a few weeks ago - she managed to fight them off. A week later, four knife-wielding men knocked at her cardboard door at an ungodly hour…smashing it in with ease. One attempted to stab her and she screamed which drew the attention of other shack dwellers who assaulted the assailant. He has been hospitalized and she receives regular death threats - if he should die, she will die too. She says her assailants are from the nearby Denver Hostel. She reported the matter to the DHS and the police - nothing has been done to move her to safety. This despite the fact there is a disability grant in the emergency guidelines meant to cater to survivors like Sithembiso. She has nowhere to go and is suicidal. Shacks by Teboho Teboho has been building decent shacks for over 5 years. These Denver shacks are shoddy even for shacks. How could the City get shacks wrong? It demonstrates the complete lack of care for the survivors and demonstrates their disdain for the inner city. Teboho will assess the shack standards since the NHBRC - understandably doesn't quality assure shacks. We will also get a quote from Builders Warehouse in order to get an accurate value on how much was actually spent. Official Interview - awaiting confirmation from the City

Requested interview and information from JMPD - they shut it down saying Floyd Brink will respond.
